## 1. First-in-class -PET radiotracers for GPR39: A platform for noninvasive target engagement imaging  in vivo
- **2026-11-09** · neuroscience
- why: Develops first PET radiotracer for emerging target GPR39, enabling in vivo target engagement studies.
- topics: first in class / emerging targets
- https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.06.764940
- abstract: Disrupted zinc homeostasis is a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease. As a key zinc-sensing receptor, GPR39, a G protein-coupled receptor implicated in neurodegeneration, vascular regulation, and neuropsychiatric disorders, represents an emerging target for molecular imaging. However, the lack of suitable positron emission tomography (PET) radiotracers has limited the in vivo characterization of GPR39. Quantitative assessment of GPR39 in vivo could improve our understanding of its role in physiology and disease and facilitate the development and evaluation of targeted therapeutics. Here, we introduce [18F]GPR39 2.1 as a PET radiotracer for specific imaging of GPR39. [18F]GPR39 2.1 exhibited excellent serum stability with negligible radiometabolite formation. In vitro cell uptake studies demonstrated a 55-70% reduction in tracer uptake following pharmacological blockade. PET imaging showed rapid brain uptake, efficient blood-brain barrier penetration, and gradual washout. Blockade studies in rats demonstrated significant reductions in brain uptake of up to approximately 90% (p<0.0001) across multiple brain regions. GPR39 specificity was further validated in GPR39 knockout mice, which showed 76% (p<0.002) and 90% (p<0.0002) reductions in brain uptake by PET imaging and biodistribution, respectively. Moreover, 5xFAD transgenic mice exhibited significantly lower brain uptake by PET imaging (40%, p<0.0002) and biodistribution (77%, p<0.002), indicating sensitivity of [18F]GPR39 2.1 to disease-associated alterations in GPR39. Biodistribution studies demonstrated favorable pharmacokinetics, while autoradiography further confirmed GPR39-specific binding, consistent with the PET and biodistribution findings. Collectively, these results establish [18F]GPR39 2.1 as a stable, brain-penetrant, and highly specific PET radiotracer for noninvasive imaging of GPR39 in vivo. This work provides a translational framework for investigating GPR39 biology and supports the development of GPR39 as an imaging and therapeutic target in neurological and systemic diseases associated with GPR39 dysregulation.

## 2. Structure-based discovery of new GPR119 ligands from on-demand tera-scale chemical space
- **2026-11-10** · biochemistry
- why: Screens trillions of compounds to discover new GPR119 ligands, combining structure-based design with ultra-large virtual screening.
- topics: protein-ligand hit discovery, computational medicinal chemistry, ultra large virtual screening
- https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.08.765217
- abstract: The orphan G protein-coupled receptor GPR119 is involved in glucose homeostasis and is considered a promising target for the treatment of diabetes and other metabolic diseases. The recently solved structures of GPR119 in complex with potential endogenous lipid agonists, including oleoylethanolamide (OEA), provide a solid platform for 3D pharmacology analysis and structure-based ligand discovery. Here, we employed the V-SYNTHES2 approach to screen ~3 trillion on-demand compounds from Enamine xREAL chemical space to identify several new chemotypes of GPR119 agonists and antagonists. Structure-guided analog-by-catalog hit expansion of new chemotypes and stereoselective synthesis resulted in a series of full and partial agonists with low-micromolar potencies in functional assays. Cryo-EM structures of active GPR119-Gs complexes bound to three of the hits validated the docking predictions and established further SAR insights into ligand-receptor interactions, enabling the discovery of BRI-17403 and BRI-17409 agonists with EC50 values of 1.6 M and 1.3 M, respectively. These results demonstrate the utility of structure-based screening of tera-scale on-demand chemical spaces in accelerating drug discovery for therapeutically relevant orphan GPCRs.

## 3. Rapid generation of antibody conformational ensembles using machine learning
- **2026-11-09** · bioinformatics
- why: Introduces a machine learning method for rapid antibody ensemble generation, improving dynamics-aware design.
- topics: machine learning for comp chem, computational medicinal chemistry
- https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.06.764889
- abstract: We introduce Cadense, a generative framework for antibody ensemble prediction that produces diverse Fv structures from sequence, informed by conformational dynamics. While a valuable resource, static structure prediction provides only a single snapshot of dynamic proteins, whose motions influence their binding and other properties. This is particularly relevant for antibodies, an important class of molecules for drug discovery, where flexible complementarity determining region (CDR) loops are difficult to model with static approaches. Cadense addresses this gap by generating ensembles that match conformational and biophysical property distributions from molecular dynamics (MD), while reducing the computational burden from days of simulation to seconds of generation. We show Cadense ensembles can recover both apo and holo conformations of the same antibody and serve as effective input to physics-based docking, capturing the conformational flexibility important to properly model antibody antigen interactions. Together, these results establish Cadense as a useful tool for antibody conformational ensemble generation with the promise to enable faster, dynamics-aware antibody design.

## 4. DiffTernary: a Diffusion Model for Molecular Glue Ternary Complex Docking
- **2026-11-11** · bioinformatics
- why: Presents a diffusion model for molecular glue ternary complex docking, advancing computational design of this emerging modality.
- topics: machine learning for comp chem, computational medicinal chemistry, first in class / emerging targets
- https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.09.765352
- abstract: Molecular glues (MGs) modulate protein function by inducing or stabilizing protein interactions. However, accurately modeling MG ternary complexes remains challenging. Here, we present DiffTernary, a diffusion-based docking method for the joint prediction of relative protein arrangement and MG binding pose. We introduce Ternary-PDB, a dataset of 76,702 experimentally determined ternary complexes curated from the Protein Data Bank using structural filters and a release cutoff aligned with AlphaFold 3 (AF3). When trained on this dataset, DiffTernary achieved acceptable protein-protein interaction (PPI) predictions (DockQ > 0.23) for 50.0% of MGBench complexes with a single prediction, compared with 51.1% for AF3. In comparisons with AF3, OpenFold3, ESMFold2, Protenix-v1 and Protenix-v2, DiffTernary ranked second with a best-of-25 PPI prediction success rate of 78.4%, behind ESMFold2 (90.9%) and ahead of AF3 (72.7%). A separate DiffTernary model trained on TernaryDB achieved a mean DockQ of 0.306 on the 94 complexes in the TernaryDB MGD test set with a single prediction, compared with 0.228 for DeepTernary. Confidence-based selection among 40 samples yielded acceptable PPI predictions for 41.5% of complexes, compared with 30.9% for DeepTernary. An E2Former variant increased training and sampling throughput 6.90-fold and 4.37-fold, respectively, under the evaluated configurations. Together, DiffTernary and Ternary-PDB provide an efficient docking approach for MG complex prediction and a valuable structural resource for MG discovery and design.

## 5. Affinity-guided design of PDZ-binding peptides in a shared latent space
- **2026-11-13** · bioinformatics
- why: Uses deep learning in a shared latent space for affinity-guided peptide design with off-target awareness.
- topics: machine learning for comp chem, computational medicinal chemistry
- https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.11.765864
- abstract: PDZ-binding motifs (PBMs) are short C-terminal sequences that bind PDZ domains and contribute to protein localization and complex assembly. Designing PBMs could modulate these interactions while leaving most of the original protein sequence unchanged. Because PDZ recognition preferences overlap, modulating intended interactions requires considering off-target binding alongside target affinity. Computational PBM design methods generally use sequence-based affinity prediction and structure-based evaluation, but it remains challenging to guide sequence searches toward different binding objectives with a single trained model. Here, we propose a deep learning-based method to design PBMs by analytically formulating single-target, off-target-aware, and dual-target design objectives as directions in a PDZ-PBM shared latent space learned through quantitative PDZ-PBM affinity prediction. In single-target PBM redesign for DLG4-PDZ3, our method identified 100 top-ranked candidates, 84 of which were in the top 1% for experimentally measured interaction fitness in a published mutant library, compared with 64 using an existing method. In single-target de novo design of 10-residue PBMs, our method achieved the highest median in silico binding scores among the compared methods for three of the four PDZ domains tested. In off-target-aware and dual-target PBM design for PTPN3 and SCRIB-PDZ3, off-target-aware design increased between-group score differences within each domain at the cost of lower target-domain scores, whereas dual-target design yielded scores close to those of the respective single-target designs for both domains. Together, these results show that shared latent representations learned from quantitative affinities allow a single trained model to guide PBM design across different binding objectives without retraining.

## 6. Learning inhibitor interactions from protein deep mutational scanning data and deep learning models
- **2026-11-13** · biophysics
- why: Benchmarks AI models on mutational scanning data, revealing limitations in predicting inhibitor interactions.
- topics: machine learning for comp chem, computational medicinal chemistry
- https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.01.763444
- abstract: Recent advances in protein language models, geometric deep learning, and structure prediction frameworks have the potential to accelerate computational drug discovery. However, it remains unclear how well these methods generalize beyond their training sets. Mutation-dependent drug responses present a challenge to these methods because there are often large effects from relatively small perturbations. Here, we systematically benchmark diverse mutational effect and drug-target affinity prediction models using deep mutational scanning datasets spanning 11 inhibitor conditions for the MET kinase domain. Across both mutational effect prediction and drug-target affinity tasks, current AI models produce largely ligand-invariant predictions despite experimentally distinct inhibitor-dependent fitness landscapes. Ligand-aware geometric models, including LigandMPNN and LASErMPNN, partially recover experimentally validated resistance-associated hotspots, highlighting the importance of explicitly modeling protein-ligand interactions and local structural flexibility. In contrast, deep learning affinity prediction models underestimate mutation-induced changes in binding affinity. This deficiency likely reflects mutation-invariant structural priors derived from co-folded structure prediction frameworks and the absence of mutation-conditioned supervision in current affinity datasets. Finally, we further extended our analysis to several kinase-inhibitor deep mutational scanning datasets and confirm the overall trends. Our findings suggest that a primary limitation in improving performance on this task lies in the scarcity of mutation-conditioned protein-ligand training data rather than model architecture alone.

## 7. Molecular Modulation of the SAM-I Riboswitch Drives Global Dynamical Shifts
- **2026-11-10** · molecular biology
- why: Combines virtual screening and MD to study SAM-I riboswitch as an emerging RNA target for antibiotics.
- topics: computational medicinal chemistry, first in class / emerging targets
- https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.03.23.713157
- abstract: A surge in antimicrobial resistance in recent years has made protein-targeting antibiotics less effective against key pathogens. It is possible to expand the range of therapeutic targets by using RNA-based therapies, but it remains necessary to improve the molecular-level understanding of interactions between RNA and known and potential binders. The SAM-I riboswitch, which controls the transcriptional termination of gene expression involved in sulfur metabolism in most bacteria, is an excellent ligand target. Thus, understanding its behavior with and without ligand complexes would be helpful for drug design. Here, we studied the interactions between the SAM-I riboswitch and its natural ligand, SAM, which controls riboswitch function, and compared those to its interactions with the similar small molecule SAH, which does not control riboswitch function, and to its interactions with a potential binder JS4, identified via virtual screening. From our simulations, we deepen understanding of small molecule interactions with the SAM-I riboswitch on both a local and a distal level. The results reveal how differently ligands (SAM, SAH and JS4) can bind to and potentially induce conformational changes in the riboswitch. Our findings offer valuable insight into the molecular mechanisms underlying riboswitch RNA-ligand interactions for the design of more effective RNA-targeting therapeutics.

## 8. ProLigGPT: a language model for protein-targeted ligand design free from structural constraints
- **2026-11-12** · bioinformatics
- why: Introduces a language model for target-specific ligand generation, directly relevant to ML-driven drug design.
- topics: machine learning for comp chem, computational medicinal chemistry
- https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2023.06.29.543848
- abstract: The deep-learning language model offers promising approaches to molecular design. However, existing models typically exhibit one or more of the following limitations: structural constraints, confinement to a single task, and lack of cross-domain capability (e.g., protein-to-ligand generation). Inspired by GPT's success in language modeling, we introduce ProLigGPT, a seq2seq autoregressive model based on GPT-2 and trained on ~1.9 million protein-ligand pairs without 3D structures. ProLigGPT supports tasks including de novo ligand generation and scaffold-based molecular design for target proteins. Benchmarking against three state-of-the-art structure-based models across eight representative target proteins, ProLigGPT demonstrated superior performance on comprehensive metrics. Through systematic evaluations of ProLigGPT's interpretability, we find that ProLigGPT uses the full protein sequence to generate target-aware ligands, unlike pocket-based strategies that depend only on residues near the binding site. Applying ProLigGPT to Pl3Kalpha; inhibitor design successfully yielded inhibitors with a novel scaffold and inhibitors derived from a known scaffold, demonstrating that ProLigGPT can reach beyond the boundaries of known chemical space. Finally, we validated the generalization ability of ProLigGPT on Target T1, which lacks a crystal structure and known inhibitors, confirming that ProLigGPT can design inhibitors solely from sequence information. These findings highlight the promise of language models in designing ligands for target proteins free from structural constraints, offering a flexible and scalable framework for exploring vast chemical spaces in drug discovery.

## 9. Pocket similarity guided selection of protein targets for systematic protein ligand dataset generation
- **2026-11-11** · bioinformatics
- why: Uses pocket similarity to select targets for binding dataset generation, aiding ML and hit discovery for understudied proteins.
- topics: protein-ligand hit discovery, machine learning for comp chem, computational medicinal chemistry, first in class / emerging targets
- https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.10.765562
- abstract: The scarcity of large, diverse, and unbiased protein ligand binding datasets limits the performance of machine learning approaches in drug discovery, particularly for understudied proteins. The Target 2035 initiative aims to address this gap by generating open-access binding data for more than 2,000 human proteins, a goal whose value depends on maximizing the diversity of the selected targets. Because proteins with different folds can share chemically analogous binding sites, we reasoned that pocket similarity, rather than sequence or fold similarity, is the appropriate criterion for selecting representative targets that maximize coverage of the human pocketome. Here, we use PocketVec, an alignment-free descriptor of binding sites, to map the human globular pocketome, identifying 51,535 predicted druggable pockets across 15,559 proteins. A two level hierarchical clustering, first within protein families and then across the whole proteome, grouped these pockets into 1,865 clusters of chemically similar binding sites. After discarding 533 clusters containing pockets with known ligands, we selected the 100 most populated of the remaining 1,332 ligand free clusters and chose two high quality representative pockets per cluster, ranked by their resemblance to known ligand-binding sites. Finally, we implemented two complementary prioritization strategies, one favoring structurally unexplored proteins and the other proteins amenable to experimental follow up, and selected 200 pockets from 100 different clusters from each strategy, with 89 clusters in common. Both selections cover over 10,000 pockets in ~5,600 proteins, approximately 36% of the human proteins with annotated druggable pockets, which represents a 2.8- to 4.4-fold increase in the number of covered pockets, domains, and proteins than random selection baselines. This pocket based framework offers a principled strategy to select diverse targets for Target 2035 and other large scale protein ligand data generation efforts in chemical biology.

## 10. Denaturation-sensitive BRET probes enable intracellular thermal shift measurements across diverse protein targets and biomolecular complexes
- **2026-11-11** · pharmacology and toxicology
- why: Presents a novel thermal shift assay for target engagement in cells, applicable to hit discovery and emerging targets.
- topics: protein-ligand hit discovery, first in class / emerging targets
- https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.10.765695
- abstract: Thermal shift assays have revolutionized drug discovery, but can be limited in sensitivity and scalability. Combining the unique attributes of differential scanning fluorimetry (DSF) and cellular thermal shift (CETSA), we report the methodological framework for the bioluminescence resonance energy transfer shift assay (BRETSA). BRETSA utilizes denaturation sensitive BRET probes, in combination with luciferase-tagged target proteins, to track and longitudinally record thermal shift in living cells. Denaturation profiles were successfully measured for over 500 globular proteins, spanning 24 target families in diverse cellular compartments. Among these, target engagement was confirmed for over 200 proteins; including validated drug targets as well as understudied members of the kinase subfamily. Leveraging orthosteric, allosteric, and covalent ligands in potency studies, this method offers improved sensitivity and scalability compared to other thermal shift methods. We extend the utility of BRETSA to interrogate target engagement at biomolecular complexes and query cooperative binding for molecular glues and emerging tricomplex drug modalities.

## 11. Methylene blue modulates G3BP1-associated condensation and attenuates Kras-driven pancreatic preneoplastic lesions
- **2026-11-12** · cancer biology
- why: Combines docking and MD to identify a modulator of condensates, relevant to computational medicinal chemistry and emerging targets.
- topics: computational medicinal chemistry, protein-ligand hit discovery, first in class / emerging targets
- https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.09.765332
- abstract: Abstract Stress granules (SGs) are dynamic biomolecular condensates implicated in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), with G3BP1/2 serving as key regulators of their assembly. We combined structure-based screening of FDA-approved drugs with cellular and biochemical assays and identified methylene blue (MB) as a modulator of SG assembly. MB suppressed SG accumulation across multiple PDAC cell lines under arsenite (AS)-induced stress, nutrient deprivation, and heat shock without reducing the abundance of major SG-associated proteins. In reconstituted systems, MB inhibited G3BP1 condensation with or without added RNA and showed a nonsignificant trend toward lower G3BP1-Caprin1 co-immunoprecipitation in cells. Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations predicted a potential MB interaction site within the G3BP1 NTF2-like (NTF2L) domain. The G3BP1 V11A/F15A/F33A/F124A mutant retained basal condensate-forming capacity but showed reduced responsiveness to MB compared with wild-type G3BP1, implicating this region in MB-mediated regulation. In Kras-driven KC mice, chronic oral MB administration was associated with reduced pancreatic G3BP1-positive puncta, increased acinar preservation, and decreased preneoplastic lesion burden, epithelial proliferation, and stromal remodeling, without overt abnormalities in the evaluated endpoints. Together, these findings identify MB as a small-molecule probe that modulates G3BP1 condensation dynamics and demonstrate that chronic MB treatment is associated with the attenuation of early Kras driven pancreatic preneoplastic lesion progression in vivo.

## 12. Thienothiazolocarboxamides: rapidly cidal agents causing catastrophic thiol collapse in Mycobacterium tuberculosis
- **2026-11-09** · microbiology
- why: Identifies a new hit for tuberculosis with a unique mechanism of action, relevant to hit discovery and first-in-class chemotypes.
- topics: protein-ligand hit discovery, first in class / emerging targets
- https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.06.764870
- abstract: Thienothiazolocarboxamides (TTCs) were discovered as a hit in a whole cell screen for new antituberculosis agents. These molecules were rapidly cidal under both replicating and non-replicating conditions and killed Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) in macrophages. The heterobicyclic core of this scaffold was essential for activity and resistance to these agents was mediated by loss of EthA, a flavin containing monooxygenase also responsible for the bioactivation of ethionamide. EthA-mediated activation of TTCs in whole cells was found to produce mycothiol adducts and RNAseq profiles revealed a mechanism of action identical to the fungal mycotoxins patulin and nidulalin A. EthA oxidizes the sulfur of the thiazole ring to create a relatively stable sulfenic acid that reacts with cellular thiols. This unique, replication-independent, mechanism suggests the possibility that these molecules may contribute significantly to shortening the duration of tuberculosis chemotherapy.

## 13. Miniaturized Traceless Staudinger Ligation Enables Direct-to-Biology Screening of Potent BRD4 PROTACs
- **2026-11-10** · cancer biology
- why: Presents a direct-to-biology platform for PROTAC synthesis and screening, advancing targeted protein degradation.
- topics: first in class / emerging targets, protein-ligand hit discovery
- https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.07.765033
- abstract: Direct-to-biology (D2B) approaches accelerate PROTAC discovery by enabling biological screening of crude reaction mixtures without intermediate purification. However, the range of chemical transformations compatible with these workflows remains limited. Herein, we establish a miniaturized, base-free traceless Staudinger ligation platform diversifying linker chemistry for a preexisting library of E3-ligand-linker adducts bearing azide moieties. As a proof-of-concept target, BRD4 was chosen, yielding amide-linked BRD4-targeting PROTACs. By combining phosphine-functionalized JQ1 derivatives with 72 selected azide building blocks, reactions were performed on a 5 L scale in 384-well plates, achieving a mean LC-MS conversion of approximately 65%. Spiking experiments confirmed that the phosphine starting materials had no significant impact on BRD4 degradation, supporting the direct biological evaluation of crude reaction mixtures in the presence of residual starting material. Cellular screening identified 23 hits at 250 nM screening concentration, reducing BRD4 levels below 40%. Two resynthesized and purified PROTACs were subsequently validated, displaying pDC50 values of 8.2 and 7.0 and a Dmax of 90% and 96%, respectively. This work establishes traceless Staudinger ligation as a complementary D2B strategy for the rapid discovery of amide-linked PROTACs.

## 14. Automated Continuous LLM-driven Biomedical Literature Mining for a Large-Scale Hepatotoxicity Knowledge Base
- **2026-11-10** · bioinformatics
- why: Uses LLM-based literature mining to build a hepatotoxicity database and trains QSAR models for ADMET prediction.
- topics: machine learning for comp chem, computational medicinal chemistry
- https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.09.765369
- abstract: Predicting whether a chemical disturbs liver and mitochondrial function matters for drug safety and environmental risk assessment, but the data available for training such models are small and mostly curated by hand. We describe an automated pipeline that uses a large language model (LLM) to collect hepatotoxicity findings from the biomedical literature. The pipeline runs a PubMed/PMC query, downloads the matching full texts or abstracts, asks the LLM to record each reported effect in a fixed schema (tested chemical, biomarker, direction of change, and related fields) with controlled vocabularies, and writes de-duplicated records to a database that is updated as new papers appear. The current snapshot holds 189,212 findings on 17,002 chemicals from 53,575 articles (1995-2026), covering 235 biomarkers reported for at least 20 chemicals. In a manual check of 217 findings from 35 articles, 208 findings (from 33 articles) were fully correct; the other 9, all from 2 articles, were incorrect. As a use case, we train structure-based QSAR models, both graph neural networks and classic baselines, for each biomarker; at this data scale the classic models remain competitive. The pipeline and the knowledge base will be made publicly available.

## 15. Cross-state representation learning enables prospective discovery of dynamic protein allosteric sites
- **2026-11-10** · bioinformatics
- why: Develops a deep learning method for allosteric site prediction, enabling discovery of cryptic pockets for drug design.
- topics: machine learning for comp chem, computational medicinal chemistry, first in class / emerging targets
- https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.09.765238
- abstract: Allosteric regulation offers multifunctional induction in therapeutic interventions, yet conformational plasticity hinders computational identification of allosteric sites. Machine learning models rely on static holo (ligand-bound) structures, generalizing poorly to apo or substrate-bound states where binding pockets are transient or cryptic. We present AsBench2, a cross-state site-recognition benchmark, and AllositeUltra, a deep learning framework integrating multimodal protein representations (combining structure-aware language models with physical dynamics) and residue-guided candidate supplementation, effectively decoupling site detection from static pocket geometry. AllositeUltra demonstrates superior generalization, achieving Top-3 site recovery rates of 65.2% and 70.6% on apo and substrate-bound structures, respectively, representing relative improvements of 36.4% and approximately 50% over the best-performing baselines. Prospective application to MAGI2 identifies a previously unrecognized interdomain allosteric pocket, validated at atomic resolution through small-molecule screening and X-ray crystallography. Proteome-wide application yields a high-confidence atlas of targetable allosteric sites, bridging the gap between structural representation learning and prospective AI-driven drug discovery.

## 16. RNA Small-Molecule Binding-Site Prediction by Integrating RNA Language Models and Structural Geometry
- **2026-11-11** · bioinformatics
- why: Proposes a deep learning model for RNA-small molecule binding site prediction, supporting RNA-targeted drug discovery.
- topics: protein-ligand hit discovery, machine learning for comp chem, computational medicinal chemistry, first in class / emerging targets
- https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.10.765632
- abstract: RNAs are emerging as promising therapeutic targets, and small-molecule binding can modulate their structure and function, creating opportunities for therapeutic development. Accurate identification of RNA small-molecule binding sites is therefore important for understanding RNA-ligand interactions and facilitating RNA-targeted drug discovery. However, the structural complexity of RNA and the limited availability of experimentally characterized RNA-ligand complexes pose challenges for computational binding-site prediction. In this study, we propose RSMBind, a graph attention-based deep learning framework for nucleotide-level prediction of RNA-small molecule binding sites. The model integrates geometric descriptors of the local three-dimensional environment with pretrained RNA language model embeddings to capture complementary structural and sequence information. We investigate three pretrained RNA language models RNA-BERT, ERNIE-RNA and RNA-FM and assess the contributions of sequence representations and geometric features through feature-level ablation experiments. The model is developed using the TR60 and HARIBOSS datasets and evaluated on four independent benchmark datasets: RB9, TE18, TL12 and JL10. RSMBind achieves the highest MCC among the compared methods on three of the four benchmarks, with relative improvements of 17.1% on RB9, 7.2% on TL12 and 16.0% on JL10 over the best previously reported results, while achieving competitive performance on TE18. Furthermore, RSMBind retains predictive capability when using only pretrained RNA language model embeddings, highlighting their potential utility when explicit tertiary structural features are unavailable. Structural analysis indicates differences in prediction performance across RNA structural regions, with loop-associated binding sites generally being captured more effectively than those embedded within stem regions. Additionally, 100 ns molecular dynamics simulations of selected RNA-ligand complexes provide insights into the relationship between predicted binding probabilities and dynamic ligand proximity, further highlighting the role of conformational dynamics in evaluating structure-based predictions. The source code is available at [ https://github.com/sharma-nandita/RSMBind].

## 17. Uncovering Features of ProteinMPNN with Sparse Autoencoders
- **2026-11-11** · bioengineering
- why: Uses sparse autoencoders to interpret ProteinMPNN and improve protein design, relevant to ML for computational chemistry and medicinal chemistry.
- topics: machine learning for comp chem, computational medicinal chemistry
- https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.09.765161
- abstract: Customization and modification of machine learning derived sequences can be achieved by understanding the mechanics behind state-of-the-art protein design models such as ProteinMPNN. Uninterpretability is hypothesized to be due largely to polysemanticity where neural networks store more features than they have dimensions. Here, we introduce sparse autoencoders (SAEs) into ProteinMPNN which expand its latent space and uncovers correlations between the activations in sparse dimensions and the presence of protein features such as secondary structure, residue volume, residue shape, disulfide bridges, and coordination to ligands. Additionally, we show that sparse activations can be manipulated to produce a variant of the short chain variable fragment Brolucizumab that is more thermostable than variants produced by traditional machine learning methods based on high temperature molecular dynamics simulations. Thus, SAEs provide both mechanistic understanding of protein design models and allow customizable manipulation of sequence prediction.

## 18. Astex-Faro: improving detection of ligand binding in cryo-EM maps through statistical baseline analysis
- **2026-11-12** · biophysics
- why: Presents a statistical framework for detecting ligand binding in cryo-EM maps, directly aiding fragment screening and hit discovery.
- topics: protein-ligand hit discovery, computational medicinal chemistry
- https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.03.763890
- abstract: Cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) is emerging as a tool for large-scale ligand screening and fragment-based drug discovery, generating extensive collections of reconstructions. At the same time, the systematic inspection of local density variations remains challenging, particularly when identifying weak or partially occupied features. Here, we present Astex-Faro, a statistical framework that defines an expected specimen state from a reference ensemble and identifies significant structural deviations in a target map through comparison against this reference. Furthermore, the method allows the enhancement of weak or poorly resolved features, enabling the recovery of signals that would otherwise be difficult to interpret. Fourier Shell Coherence (FSCoh) is introduced as a metric that quantifies consistency across reconstruction ensembles. We show that Astex-Faro reliably detects subtle structural features and improves their interpretability across datasets spanning a broad range of experimental challenges, from highly homogeneous specimens to membrane proteins, low-occupancy ligands and fragment-screening experiments. Together, these developments provide a practical framework for cryo-EM screening, increasing confidence in hit identification and reducing the risk of missed binding events.

## 19. RNAtomy: A Structure-Aware RNA Foundation Model for Transferable Structural and Functional Representations
- **2026-11-12** · bioengineering
- why: Introduces a structure-aware RNA foundation model that could enable drug discovery targeting RNA, an emerging target class.
- topics: machine learning for comp chem, first in class / emerging targets
- https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.10.765792
- abstract: RNA plays a critical and diverse role in gene expression, catalysis, regulation, and molecular recognition. This functional versatility arises from the interplay between nucleotide sequence, structural organization, and cellular context. Nevertheless, most RNA foundation models are pretrained primarily using sequence or secondary-structure information, while the systematic integration of three-dimensional geometric and conformational features remains comparatively underexplored. Here, we introduce RNAtomy, a self-supervised RNA foundation model designed to learn the structural anatomy of RNA from inter-nucleotide geometry and residue-level conformational descriptors. Its design has three main components: 1) joint masked reconstruction of pairwise geometry and residue-level descriptors to connect spatial organization with local conformation; 2) a hybrid Mamba-Transformer backbone in which Mamba blocks efficiently propagate global context, while shifted-window attention compensates for the absence of explicit content-dependent token interactions in Mamba by modeling relationships within local regions of the pairwise map; and 3) axis-aware feature-wise linear modulation that maps nucleotide-level conformations to the row and column axes of pairwise geometry. We assess RNAtomy across seven diverse tasks involving structural and functional predictions at the nucleotide, nucleotide-pair, and RNA levels. RNAtomy achieved particularly strong performance on structural tasks, outperforming established RNA foundation models and task-specific approaches in contact and long-range base-pair prediction. Its representations also transferred effectively to interaction-related tasks, despite the substantial differences between these applications and the structural pretraining objective. On functional tasks, RNAtomy achieved superior performance in translation-related prediction and regulatory-element identification. Notably, RNAtomy achieved these results despite being pretrained on a substantially smaller training set than the RNA foundation models used as baselines. Together, these results highlight how rich structural information, when learned through an expressive architecture, can support transferable RNA representations across biologically distinct structural and functional applications.

## 20. Uncovering Features of ProteinMPNN with Sparse Autoencoders
- **2026-11-13** · bioengineering
- why: Same as [1], uses sparse autoencoders to interpret ProteinMPNN and improve protein design.
